original_value: Computational models for sarcasm detection have often relied on the content of utterances in isolation. However, the speaker’s sarcastic intent is not always apparent without additional context. Focusing on social media discussions, we investigate three issues: (1) does modeling conversation context help in sarcasm detection? (2) can we identify what part of conversation context triggered the sarcastic reply? and (3) given a sarcastic post that contains multiple sentences, can we identify the specific sentence that is sarcastic? To address the first issue, we investigate several types of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks that can model both the conversation context and the current turn. We show that LSTM networks with sentence-level attention on context and current turn, as well as the conditional LSTM network, outperform the LSTM model that reads only the current turn. As conversation context, we consider the prior turn, the succeeding turn, or both. Our computational models are tested on two types of social media platforms: Twitter and discussion forums. We discuss several differences between these data sets, ranging from their size to the nature of the gold-label annotations. To address the latter two issues, we present a qualitative analysis of the attention weights produced by the LSTM models (with attention) and discuss the results compared with human performance on the two tasks.

result.paraphrase: Computational models for sarcasm detection have often depended on utterances in isolation. Yet a speaker’s sarcastic intent is not always clear without extra context. Using social media discussions, we examine three questions: (1) does incorporating conversation context improve sarcasm detection? (2) can we determine which part of the conversation context prompted the sarcastic reply? and (3) for a sarcastic post with multiple sentences, can we identify the specific sarcastic sentence? To answer the first question, we explore several Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network variants that model both the conversation context and the current turn. We find that LSTMs with sentence-level attention over the context and current turn, along with the conditional LSTM network, outperform an LSTM that considers only the current turn. For conversation context, we use the prior turn, the following turn, or both. We evaluate our computational models on two social media settings: Twitter and discussion forums. We also discuss several differences between these datasets, from size to the nature of the gold-label annotations. To address the last two questions, we provide a qualitative analysis of the attention weights generated by the attention-based LSTM models and compare the results with human performance on the two tasks.
